What is a copy constructor and why do we need it?

A copy constructor is a special member function that initializes a new object as a copy of an existing one. It's invoked when you pass an object by value, return one from a function, or explicitly create a copy. The compiler provides a default version that copies each member, but this can be dangerous when your class manages resources like memory. For example, if your class contains a raw pointer, the default copy constructor will copy the pointer's address—not the data it points to—leading to two objects sharing the same memory. This is called a shallow copy. [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/copy_constructor)

This preserves the dynamic type and prevents slicing. Can you explain the Rule of Three? Why do I need to implement all three if I only want a custom destructor?

The Rule of Three arises in C++ when a class manages a resource, like dynamic memory. If you define one of these three — destructor, copy constructor, or copy assignment operator — you likely need to define all three. Why? Because the default behavior for copying (both construction and assignment) performs a shallow copy: it copies pointers, not the data they point to. If your destructor frees that memory, then two objects pointing to the same memory can lead to double deletion or dangling pointers. So even if you only think you need a custom destructor, the act of managing memory implies you must also control how copying works. [1](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/notes/2/)
Before we look at the code again, could you explain the general concept we're using here?

Think of a class managing dynamic memory like being the owner of a house. The destructor is like your will — it says what happens to the house when you're gone. But what happens when you make a copy of yourself? The default copy just gives the copy a deed to the same house. Now two people think they own it. When one dies, they destroy the house — and the other person’s deed is now worthless. That’s a dangling pointer. The copy constructor lets you build a new house for the copy, and the assignment operator lets you transfer ownership safely. This is why all three must work together: they manage ownership. [1](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/notes/2/)
